newsitem.title: INDIA: Lower interest boosts India HLL profits.
newsitem.headline: Lower interest boosts India HLL profits.

text.p: Lower interest costs and tax rates boosted first half profits of Hindustan Lever Ltd (HLL) and analysts said on Tuesday they expect the multinational firm to maintain the growth for the whole year.
"We're forecasting 20 percent top-line growth for 1997 and bottomline growth of 27 percent," an analyst at Peregrine Capital India said.
Company analyst Nishid Shah at Inquire India Equity Research, a division of Motilal Oswal Securities Ltd, forecast sales to grow 25 percent and net profit 28 percent in calendar 1997.
Hindustan Lever is the Indian subsidiary of Anglo-Dutch conglomerate Unilever Plc.
The firm said on Tuesday its net profit in the six months to June 30 totalled 2.56 billion rupees -- slightly higher than expected by analysts -- on sales of 38.9 billion rupees.

"Sales were bang on target but our profit estimates were off two percent," said Swapna Naik, analyst at HSBC Batlivala & Karani Securities. "Net margins rose from 6.0 percent to 6.6 percent because of lower interest and tax rates."

The net profit and sales in the first half of 1996 were 18.5 billion rupees and 32.8 billion respectively, but these were before the merger of affiliate Brooke Bond Lipton India Ltd with Hindustan Lever was completed.
In the first six months to June 30, interest costs fell 35.4 percent to 184.0 million rupees from 284.8 million in the year-ago period, the firm said.
The firm's directors set an interim dividend of 7.5 rupees per 10-rupee face stock. For 1996 it had paid a total dividend of 12.5 percent, including interim of 6.0 percent.
Hindustan Lever shares rose 17.5 rupees to 1,533 on the Bombay Stock Exchange on Tuesday.
"Interest savings are significant and commendable," said one analyst at an Europeon securities firm. "It reflects much better funds position and working capital management."
The company was also benefited by a cut in corporate tax rates to 35 percent from an effective 42.5 percent by the Indian government in its budget for fiscal 1997/98 (April-March).
The analyst said he planned to raise his net profit projections for calendar 1997 to 5.4 billion rupees from earlier estimate of 5.3 billion. The firm made a net profit of 4.1 billion rupees in 1996.
Peregrine will stick to its forecast of 5.2 billion rupees.
Volumes growth in detergents, strong margins in personal care products, better markets for coffee and tea would have contributed to profits, analysts said.
The company is shifting its focus to food products and analysts see this sector as the major contributor to its profits in future.
"It is now in an investment phase," said Inquire's Shah. "I see enormous potential for an upside."
The company said it was investing in building up brands for new ice-creams and culinary products like tomato-chilli sauce, wheat flour and salt.

"The future prospects of growth and profitability in these two businesses are promising but building critical mass and streamlining the supply chain will require much investment for the next few years," a company statement said.
Analysts expect the foods business to provide the engine for growth in years ahead.
"In four-to-five years foods would account for 50 percent of total business," one analyst said.
